input.title: The Wine-Dark Debt
input.world_description:
The harbour of **Aktoria** sits in the crook of a limestone bay where two rivers of legend are said to meet the sea, though no map agrees on where. It is a working port first and a holy place second, though the two have long since grown into each other: net-menders hang their catch to dry on the plinths of drowned heroes, and the customs house is built from the timbers of ships that never should have made it home. The town clings to the slopes above the water in tiers of whitewashed stone gone grey with salt, its streets narrow enough that two loaded mules cannot pass without one backing into a doorway, and everywhere the smell of tar, fish-brine, and the incense burned to keep the harbour's temper sweet.

Aktoria's founding myth, told a hundred slightly different ways in a hundred dockside wineshops, concerns *two men named Ajax*, both heroes of the great war across the sea, who came home by this same channel and met two entirely different fates. The greater of them, grief-maddened and betrayed by his own countrymen over a dead man's armor, is said to have fallen on his sword somewhere on the headland now called **Aianteion**, and his blood is why the wild iris there blooms red instead of purple. The lesser of them, arrogant and sacrilegious, dragged a captive priestess from a goddess's altar during the war's sack and paid for it on the voyage home: his ship broken on the Kapherid rocks just past the harbour mouth, and when he boasted that he had survived the sea god's wrath despite the gods, the sea itself is said to have opened beneath him and taken him down still boasting. Two heroes, two harbours' worth of story, one name — and the town has spent generations arguing about which Ajax deserves the bigger festival, which Ajax the harbour actually belongs to, and which Ajax's unfinished business is the reason ships still sometimes do not come back.

Because they do not always come back. Past the twin headlands that the locals call **the Ajakes** — one gentle and green, one black rock and broken teeth — the strait known as the **Kapherid Race** runs sea-mad on certain nights for no reason the pilots have ever agreed on, tides moving against wind and current both, lights seen low on the water that are not any ship's lantern. Old women who have buried sons say it is the Lesser One still boasting, still being punished, and that the sea will keep swallowing boats until someone finishes his voyage properly — makes the offering he refused to make, or carries word to the goddess he insulted, or simply sails the strait at the one hour when passage is permitted and proves it can be done without drowning. Whether that is superstition, priestcraft, or plain truth is exactly the kind of question Aktoria has stopped being able to answer, because too many disprovable claims have drowned along with the people who made them.

The town itself runs on the old rivalry, now gone civic and commercial. The **Telamon docks** on the harbour's eastern arm, named for the Greater Ajax's father, control the grain trade and the shipwrights' guild, proud, orderly, ruinously expensive, their captains sworn to a code of honor so strict it has bankrupted half of them. The **Oiliad docks** to the west, named for the Lesser Ajax's father, run the harbour's actual money — smuggling, salvage rights, the profitable business of insuring voyages that the eastern captains consider too disreputable to insure at all — fast, cunning, contemptuous of ceremony, and quietly furious that history remembers their founder only as the fool who drowned. The two guilds share the harbourmaster's office by a treaty two hundred years old and broken in some small way almost every week. A shrine sits on neutral ground at the harbour's head, two altars back to back under one roof, and it is considered extremely bad luck to pray at only one.

Into this stalemate comes the thing that finally forces the issue: a **voyage that must be made**, sanctioned by the temple, financed reluctantly by both guilds because neither trusts the other to make it alone, meant to carry an offering — old debts are vague on exactly what, which is itself part of the trouble — out past the Ajakes, through the Race, to a shrine on open water that no living pilot has actually seen, only heard described by dead ones. Whoever captains it will settle, whether they mean to or not, two hundred years of argument about which hero the harbour really honors, whether the sea can be paid off or only endured, and what exactly happened to every ship that tried this crossing before and did not send word home.
